opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it started as a grand plan. It was more that I kept noticing I was happiest when I was stuck on a problem nobody had a clean answer to yet. In a lot of settings you're handed a well-defined task and the goal is to execute it well. In research, half the work is figuring out what the right question even is, and I found that really addictive.

There's also a kind of freedom in academia that's hard to find elsewhere. You can follow your curiosity for a while without someone asking right away, "What's the quarterly impact?" That room to explore, to be wrong a few times before you're right, matters a lot to me, especially in a field moving as fast as AI systems. Some of the most useful things I've worked on came from asking a simple question, like why something was so slow or so wasteful, and then refusing to let it go.

And the people. Being around students and collaborators who are just as obsessed with a problem as you are is energizing. You argue at the whiteboard, you build something, it breaks, you fix it together. That loop of thinking, building, and sharing it openly so others can build on it is what pulled me in, and it's a big part of why I've stayed close to research even as the line between academia and industry keeps blurring.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I ever made a single big decision to go into academia. It was more a series of small moments where I realized I kept wanting to understand why something worked, not just that it worked.

When I was an undergrad, I did some internships and I enjoyed building things, but there was always this feeling of, okay, we shipped it, but I still don't really get what's going on underneath. The systems problems I found most interesting were the ones where nobody had a clean answer yet. And the place where you get to sit with those questions for a long time, and where people actually reward you for asking them, is a PhD.

The other thing was the people. I had advisors and senior students who were incredibly generous with their time. Watching them think through a problem on a whiteboard, getting it wrong, erasing it, trying again, that was very appealing to me. It felt like a community where being confused out loud was fine, as long as you were confused about something that mattered.

And then I think what kept me there, especially working on things like serving large language models, is that the line between research and real systems got very thin. You can write a paper and the next week someone is actually running your code to serve real users. That feedback loop is addictive. You're not just producing ideas, you're producing things people use, and you still get to ask the deeper questions about why. That combination is what I was looking for, even if I couldn't have named it at the time.

astra-6.text: I think it was the curiosity, and the freedom to follow that curiosity. I enjoy taking a question that I don’t fully understand and spending time working through it—trying something, finding out why it doesn’t work, and gradually getting somewhere. An academic life appealed to me because that process is central to the work. And you get to share it with people who are excited about asking questions, too.

sol-6.1.text: I think what drew me to academia was the freedom to explore questions deeply. I enjoy the process of taking something I don’t understand, breaking it down, and gradually figuring out how it works. In research, you don’t always know whether an idea will succeed, but that uncertainty is also part of the appeal. And I like being around people who are curious, who challenge your assumptions, and who help you see a problem from a different perspective.
